These lenses served long telescopes of considerable power, and Cassini made his discoveries with them. Campani also observed himself, and disputed with Eustachio Divini the priority of the spots on Jupiter, to which Cassini had called his attention. His observations and telescope descriptions appear in papers of 1664, 1665, and 1666, including letters to Cassini on the shadows of the Medicean stars on Jupiter's face.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-cata:
Giuseppe Catalani, also called Catalano or Catalanus, was a Roman liturgist of the eighteenth century and member of the Oratory of San Girolamo della Carita. He is famous for correct editions of the chief liturgical books of the Roman Church, still in habitual use, enriched with scholarly commentaries on their history, rubrics, and canon law. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows an editor of lasting authority.

Among his editions are the Pontificale Romanum in three volumes of 1738 to 1740, based on the best manuscripts. His Caeremoniale episcoporum dates to 1747, and his Rituale Romanum to 1757. He also wrote on the history, duties, and privileges of two curial offices. He edited the decrees of the ecumenical councils in a work Hurter calls very learned. His 1753 edition of Aguirre's collection of Spanish and New World councils served scholars of the Americas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-mari:
Giuseppe Maria Bernini was a Capuchin missionary and Orientalist born near Carignan in Piedmont, who died in Hindustan in 1753. For many years he served as a missionary in the East Indies and gained a remarkable knowledge of the languages and dialects of India. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a traveler who studied the peoples he met.

In his travels he studied closely the manners, customs, and religious beliefs and practices of the people. He gathered the results in his Notizie laconiche of 1747 on customs, sacrifices, and idols in the kingdom of Neipal. Never published, it is kept in manuscript at the Propaganda in Rome and in Cardinal Borgia's museum. He also wrote Dialogues in an Indian language, translated the Adhiatma Ramayana and the Djana Sagara, and compiled historical studies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-pari:
Giuseppe Parini was an Italian poet born at Bosisio on 23 May 1729, who died at Milan on 15 August 1799. Taken early to Milan, he showed marked ability for teaching, the work of most of his life, and entered the Arcadia on his poetic talent. Ordained in 1754, he tutored noble families and learned the fashionable life he would satirize. A Catholic Encyclopedia article rests his fame on the Odi and the Giorno.

From 1773 he taught fine arts at the Brera in Milan. Bonaparte made him a member of the municipal government under the Cisalpine Republic, a post he lost for his liberal utterances. The Giorno, begun about 1760, follows a society beau through morning, midday, evening, and night in unrhymed ten-syllable verse, mocking the effeminate and corrupt customs of fashionable youth. His Odi of 1791 treat moral and social questions in the conventional Arcadian manner.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-tart:
Giuseppe Tartini was a violinist, composer, and theorist born at Pirano in Italy on 12 April 1692, who died at Padua on 16 February 1770. He resisted his parents' wish that he enter the Franciscan Order, studied law at Padua from 1710, then gave it up for music and fencing. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows one of the greatest violin players of all time.

After fleeing to Assisi over a secret marriage and a charge of abduction, later dropped, he returned to Padua. He settled for years at Ancona. In 1721 he became solo violinist and orchestra conductor at Padua Cathedral, a post he held for life apart from two years at Prague. His Padua school of 1728 produced masters such as Nardini, and his manner of bowing is still standard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-zamb:
Giuseppe Zamboni was a priest and physicist born at Venice in June 1776, who died there on 25 July 1846. After studies at the Verona seminary he took the chair of physics in the city's lyceum. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the inventor of the dry pile that still rings bells at Oxford.

His dry pile of 1812 stacked paper discs, zinc foil on one face and manganese binoxide on the reverse, with the paper's own moisture serving as conductor. Pressed in a glass tube, the stack gave force enough to deflect an electroscope's leaves. With a light brass ball swinging between the terminal knobs he made an electric clock. At Oxford's Clarendon Laboratory such a pile has rung bells continuously for fifty years, though it is no perpetual motor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregario-meng:
Gregario Mengarini was a pioneer missionary of the Flathead tribe and philologist of their language, born at Rome on 21 July 1811, who died at Santa Clara, California, on 23 September 1886. He entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1828 at barely seventeen and taught grammar at Rome, Medina, and Reggio. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a volunteer moved by the Flatheads' appeal.

Hearing Bishop Rosati's letter read in the refectory in 1839, he volunteered at once. He was ordained in March 1840 and sailed from Leghorn in July with Father Cotling. With De Smet's party he journeyed by river and trail to Fort Hall in August 1841. Then he reached the Saint Mary's River site in Montana, where the missionaries cut frozen earth with axes to found a log mission plastered with clay and thatched with weeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregorio-panz:
Gregorio Panzani was Bishop of Mileto, who died early in 1662. A secular priest of Arezzo who had left the Oratory for ill health, he was chosen by Cardinal Barberini in 1634 for a secret agency in London. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a man of experienced virtue, singular address, and polite learning.

His commission was to report firsthand on divided English Catholics. He was to settle differences between seculars and regulars over the oath of allegiance and a vicar Apostolic, and open informal relations with the government. He reconciled seculars with Benedictines and other religious, but the Jesuits stayed out. He met secretaries Windebank and Cottington, won the queen's confidence, and was admitted to secret audience with the king. Elected Bishop of Mileto on 13 August 1640, he left memoirs whose authenticity was later questioned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregory-of-ri:
Gregory of Rimini was an Augustinian theologian born at Rimini in the second half of the thirteenth century, who died at Vienna in 1358. After teaching at home he was called to Paris to a professorship at the Sorbonne, where he won great distinction as a teacher. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a chief leader of the Nominalists.

His disciples called him Doctor acutus, Lucerna splendens, and especially Doctor authenticus, and many called him beatus for his erudition and heroic virtue. A pertinacious champion of Saint Augustine on grace and original sin, he opposed the general Scholastic teaching, even against the Aegidian school he belonged to. His opponents called him Infantium Tortor, tormentor of children, for his severe view of unbaptized children. He became General of the Augustinian Hermits in 1357 and died the next year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guido-reni:
Bologna's Guido Reni, born at Calvenzano in 1575, was once among the most prized painters in Europe, though fashion later dimmed his name. Trained by Calvaert and the Carracci, he worked in Rome on the Farnese and Quirinal palaces and Borghese chapel. His ceiling of Phoebus and the Hours before Aurora in the Palazzo Rospigliosi stands as his Roman high point.

Early pictures show pure colour and dramatic force, while later success brought a fluent but thinner manner that has hurt their survival. An engraver and etcher as well as a fresco and panel painter, he left works scattered from Dresden and St. Petersburg to many English country houses, and the entry expects his skill in composition and drawing to win fresh regard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-in-coena-domi:
In Coena Domini names a papal Bull read each year in Rome on Maundy Thursday, the feast of the Lord's Supper. In St. Peter's loggia, before pope, cardinals, and Roman Court, an auditor of the Sacred Roman Rota read it in Latin, and a cardinal-deacon then read it in Italian. Once read, the pope threw a burning wax torch down into the piazza.

Inside were excommunication censures for many offences, with absolution kept to the pope alone. Publishing censures on a set cycle was an old habit. In 1195 York's council told priests to proclaim censures on perjurers three times a year, with bell and lit candle. London's council in 1200 ordered yearly proclamation against sorcerers, perjurers, arsonists, thieves, and rapists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-bellarin:
John Bellarini was an Italian Barnabite theologian best known as a moral theologian of the Counter-Reformation. Born at Castelnuovo in 1552, he served as visitor and twice as assistant general of his order. At Padua and Rome he taught theology. Bishops and cardinals held him in high esteem, particularly Gregory XV.

His most valuable work is a two-part commentary on the Council of Trent, and on the Roman Catechism. One volume instructs the faithful in the Apostles' Creed; it was published at Brescia in 1603. Another, aimed at converting heretics, was published at Milan in 1620 and often reprinted. He also wrote Italian booklets for confessors and penitents, a treatise on St. Thomas's doctrine of predetermination, a work on method, and a Mirror of Divine and Human Wisdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-cassan:
Joseph Cassani was a Spanish Jesuit scholar who helped found Madrid's Academy of the Spanish Language. Born at Madrid in 1673, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1686 and became an Academy member in 1713. He worked on the Academy's great Dictionary of the Castilian Language, published in six volumes from 1726 to 1730.

Cassani was a prolific author on saints' lives, fortification, and comets. His most valued book for Americans is his 1741 history of the Jesuit province of New Granada, the only regular chronicle of the order in Colombia. Though he never crossed the Atlantic, the work gives a careful account of missions in the upper Orinoco basin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-pitoni:
Joseph Pitoni was an Italian church musician who led the choirs of Rome's greatest basilicas. Born at Rieti in 1657, he began music study at Rome at five and, still under sixteen, wrote pieces sung at the Holy Apostles. He directed choirs at Monte Rotondo and Assisi, returned to Rome in 1677, and became director of St. John Lateran in 1708.

In 1719 Pitoni became choirmaster of St. Peter's, a post he held for twenty-four years. He could write each voice part separately without a full score, and his output, much of it for three and four choirs, was called infinite by his pupil Chiti. He began a Mass for twelve choirs but age kept him from finishing it. He died at Rome in 1743.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lazzaro-spall:
Lazzaro Spallanzani (1729-1799) was a distinguished eighteenth-century Italian scientist, born at Scandiano in Modena and schooled at Reggio's Jesuit college. Under his cousin Laura Bassi, Bologna's famed woman professor of natural philosophy, he left law, took priestly orders, and at twenty-five taught logic, metaphysics, and Greek at Reggio.

Chairs at Coimbra, Parma, and Cesena beckoned, but he chose Modena in 1760 and gave spare hours to natural science. In 1768 Maria Theresa drew him to Pavia's reorganized natural history chair, where he enriched the museum with Swiss and Mediterranean collections. His biology counted most: classic studies of regeneration showed lizards and snails regrowing lost parts, the land snail even its head, with eyes, mouth, tongue, and teeth, though not its brain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leonardo-brun:
Leonardo Bruni (1369-1444), called Aretino, was an Italian humanist of poor parents. He began in law, then, under Chrysoloras, turned to the classics. In 1405 his friend Poggio won him the post of Apostolic secretary under Innocent VII. He stayed at Rome under Gregory XII and Alexander V. Elected Chancellor of Florence in 1410, he resigned after a few months and returned to the papal court under John XXIII.

On that pope's deposition in 1415 Bruni returned to Florence. There he wrote his chief work, the twelve-book Latin history of Florence, for which the State gave him citizenship and tax freedom. In 1427 he was again made chancellor until his death. He opened Greek treasures to Latin scholars with literal translations of Aristotle, Plato, Plutarch, Demosthenes, and Aeschines. He also wrote lives of Dante, Petrarch, Cicero, and Aristotle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leopoldo-marc:
Leopoldo Marco Antonio Caldani (1725-1813) was an anatomist born at Bologna. He studied medicine there and took his degree in 1750. In 1755 he became professor of practical medicine at Bologna. The post required five more years of anatomy study under Morgagni. He left Bologna, apparently because of enemies, and went to Padua. As one of Morgagni's best pupils he became professor of medicine there. In 1771, after Morgagni's death, he became professor of anatomy. He held that chair until retiring in 1805.

Caldani championed Haller's theory of irritability with zeal. He is noted for experiments on the spinal cord's function and for bringing electricity into nerve study. His best known work is his anatomical atlas, made with his nephew Floriano's help. Among his books are Institutiones pathologicae, Institutiones semeioticae of 1808, and Icones anatomicae with five volumes of notes, published at Venice from 1801 to 1813.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lodovico-mazz:
Lodovico Mazzolini, also called Mazzolini da Ferrara, was an Italian painter born at Ferrara in 1480, dead by 1528 or 1530. Long classed as a pupil of Lorenzo Costa, he is better seen as a pupil of Panetti, a case Morelli proved from ears and hands, blue conical mountains, and gem-like colour.

Morelli nicknamed him the Glow-worm for his luminous, sparkling tints. Cream marble architecture marks his pictures, with gold lights on drapery and small figures that charm more than grand history scenes. His Christ among the Doctors of 1524 hangs at Berlin, with a Virgin and Child there too, and works in the Louvre, the National Gallery, and Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucovico-zacc:
Ludovico Zacconi was an Italian music theorist, born at Pesaro about 1550 and dead at Venice after 1623. An Augustinian friar ordained at Venice, he served as choirmaster there in 1585, joined Duke Wilhelm of Bavaria's chapel in 1592, and became Kapellmeister to Archduke Charles at Vienna in 1596.

His fame rests on Prattica di Musica, issued in 1592 with a second volume in 1619, four works that cover the whole of late sixteenth-century music. Rules for singing polyphony, with Palestrina examples, stand highest in value, beside full treatments of the twelve modes, instruments and their ranges, and scoring for early opera and oratorio.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luigi-gaetano:
Luigi Gaetano Marini was an Italian scholar of law, history, and antiquities, born at Sant'Arcangelo in 1742 and dead at Paris in 1815. Schooled at San Marino and Rimini, he took law and letters at Bologna with brilliance and graduated at Ravenna in both laws.

At Rome from 1764 he befriended Cardinals Albani and Garampi and kept up a wide scholars' correspondence. He rose to coadjutor, then prefect, of the archives, and in 1800 Pius VII made him first keeper of the Vatican Library. Napoleon carried the Curia archives to Paris, Marini went with them in 1810, and died there in 1815 before they reached Rome again. His papyrus work remains a standard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luigi-galvani:
Luigi Galvani was a Bolognese physician and anatomist, born in 1737 and dead in 1798. He meant to study theology and enter a monastery, but his family turned him to natural science, where he shone as surgeon and childbirth doctor.

Lecturer at Bologna and teacher of anatomy at twenty-five, he lost his wife Lucia in 1790 after thirty years of marriage. In 1798 he gave up his chair rather than swear the Cisalpine Republic's civil oath, and died in poverty before friends won him emeritus rank. His fame rests on frog-leg twitches in 1780, which led to his theory of animal electricity, a nervous fluid from brain to muscle, later dropped yet fruitful for later science.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luigi-lambrus:
Luigi Lambruschini was an Italian cardinal and diplomat, born near Genoa in 1776 and dead at Rome in 1854. A Barnabite from youth, he served as secretary to Consalvi at the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and helped frame concordats with Naples and Bavaria.

Archbishop of Genoa from 1819, nuncio to Paris from 1827 until revolution cut his mission short in 1830, he became cardinal in 1831 and Secretary of State under Gregory XVI. With the pope he dropped Benedict XIV's conciliatory line, faced Prussia over Cologne's imprisoned archbishop in 1837, and won Bunsen's recall. Next to Consalvi and Pacca, he ranks among the Holy See's great nineteenth-century diplomats.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marc-antonio-:
Marc' Antonio Franceschini was an Italian painter born at Bologna in 1648 and dead there about 1729. He is best known for decorative work at Parma, Bologna, and Genoa, and for designs made for Clement XI for mosaics in St Peter's. He belonged to the Eclectic School and followed the Carracci.

His chief works include the Ranuzzi ceiling at Bologna, two fine pictures in the Bologna Gallery, the Annunciation and the Holy Family, and a Servite convent picture of the order's founders. A few years later he painted St Thomas of Villanova giving alms for the Augustinian church at Rimini. Historians claim a Madrid visit, but most hold he declined the invitation, unwilling to leave his native land. He painted to his death, signing one Venice picture at seventy-eight and a Genoa Rebecca at eighty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marco-battagl:
Marco Battaglini was a historian of the councils, born at Rimini in 1645 and dead at Cesena in 1717. He studied civil and church law at Cesena, taking doctorates in both at sixteen. After civil service in the Papal States, he entered the priesthood. He became Bishop of Nocera in Umbria in 1690 and moved to Cesena in 1716.

He was prized for learning and for a generous, frank temper. His chief works were three. Il legista filosofo of 1680 treats the lawyer as philosopher. Istoria universale di tutti i concilii, first issued at Venice in 1686, began with 475 councils and later added 403 more, with a catalogue of ancient and current bishoprics. Annali del sacerdozio e dell' imperio of 1701 to 1711 tells world history through the seventeenth century in annals form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mario-luigi-c:
Luigi Cherubini was a composer, born at Florence in 1760 and dead at Paris in 1842. His father, a musician, taught him from age six, and by thirteen he had written a Te Deum, Credo, Miserere, Mass, and Dixit. 

That pension let him learn counterpoint and Roman-school music from Giuseppe Sarti at Bologna. Sarti told him to drop the Neapolitan School for Palestrina and his peers, and set pupils copying Roman masters' scores, a habit Cherubini kept for life and enforced as Paris Conservatoire director. Early liturgical music gave way to opera. From 1788 to 1805 he laboured in Paris through revolution and unrest, his operas Demophon, Lodoiska, Medee, and Les deux journees playing only at the small Theatre de la Foire. Disappointed, he nearly stopped composing, until a Mass in F for Chimay's church dedication in 1809 turned him back to church music, where his mature powers shone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martino-marti:
Martino Martini was a distinguished Austrian Jesuit missionary to seventeenth-century China, born at Trent in 1614 and dead at Hangzhou in 1661. He entered the Austrian province in 1631 and studied mathematics under Athanasius Kircher at the Roman College, likely aiming for China. 

In 1650 he went to Rome as procurator for the Chinese mission. On the long, adventurous voyage via the Philippines, a Dutch privateer to Batavia, and Bergen, Norway, reached 31 August 1653, he sifted his historical and cartographical data. In Europe he printed the works that made him famous, then returned in 1658 with provisionally favourable ritual instructions and laboured till death. Richthofen calls him the leading geographer of the Chinese mission, unexcelled and hardly equalled in the eighteenth century. His Novus Atlas Sinensis of 1653, seventeen maps and 171 pages, stands as the fullest geographical account of China then known, making him father of geographical learning on China.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michelangelo-:
Michelangelo Tamburini, fourteenth General of the Society of Jesus, was born at Modena on 27 September 1648 and died on 28 February 1730. After teaching scholastic philosophy and theology for twelve years, he became rector of several colleges in turn. He was chosen by Cardinal Reynold of Este as his private theologian, and held the posts of secretary general and vicar to Thyrsus Gonzalez. 

His reputation for solid virtue, patience, and courage never dimmed through his long generalate. Under Tamburini the Society's apostolic work stood at its best, yet signs of the storm that would annihilate it half a century later were already visible. Paraguay's Reductions began to bear fruit, and missionaries died for plague victims in the Levant or pressed into Tibet's steppes amid untold hardships. Peter the Great admitted Jesuits to Russia, and Jansenism, the Society's bitterest foe, took its death blow in 1708 when Clement XI suppressed Port-Royal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mino-di-giova:
Mino di Giovanni, called da Fiesole, was born in 1431 and died in 1484. He is inscribed in the Libro della Matricola of the Florentine masters of stone and woodwork as Minus Johannis Mini de Pupio. Some have concluded from this that he was born at Poppi in the Casentino, while elsewhere he appears as Mino di Giovanni di Mino da Firenze. As a sculptor he won praise for work of rare delicacy and polish.

Many portraits and low-relief pieces pass under his name. They include the circular Madonna and Child on a bracket in the Bargello, Florence, and the busts of Piero and Giovanni de' Medici there. Also his are the bust of Rinaldo della Luna dated 1461, and a remarkable portrait of Isotta da Rimini. His refined marble work made him one of the early Renaissance's most admired sculptors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-narni-and-ter:
Narni and Terni are united Central Italian dioceses. Narni is the ancient Nequinum of the Sabines. Romans besieged it in 300 and 299 BC, destroyed the city and sent a Latin colony there, and renamed it Narnia. Luitprand captured it in 726, but Pope Zacharias had him restore it to the Duchy of Rome in 742, after which it stayed under pontifical rule. From 1198 to 1214 Narni rebelled against Innocent III, who briefly suppressed its see.

Its churches hold many ancient Umbrian school paintings. Narni is the birthplace of Blessed Lucia of Narni, a Dominican tertiary who died in 1544, and of the condottiere Erasmo Gattamelata. It venerates as first bishop the martyr Juvenalis, dead in the later fourth century. Later bishops included Maximus, Cassius, noted by Saint Gregory the Great, and John, whose son became John XIII. William, used by Urban V against the Fraticelli, and Raimondo Castelli, founder of a seminary, also served.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-niccolo-alama:
Niccolo Alamanni, a Roman antiquary of Greek origin, was born at Ancona on 12 January 1583 and died in Rome in 1626. Educated in Rome at the Greek College founded by Gregory XIII, he was ordained deacon and priest by the Latin rite. After teaching Greek to persons of rank, he became secretary to Cardinal Borghese and later custodian of the Vatican Library.

His death is said to have come from too close attendance at Saint Peter's high altar erection, where he saw that martyrs' sepulchres were not disturbed. He wrote a Syntagma on the Lateran walls for restorations under Borghese, and a dissertation on right and left side precedence in old papal coins placing Saint Paul right of Saint Peter. He is best known as editor, at Lyons in 1623, of Procopius's Anecdota, or Secret History, violently criticised outside Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-niccolo-orlan:
Niccolo Orlandini, born at Florence in 1554 and dead at Rome in 1606, entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1572. He became rector at Nola, master of novices at Naples for five years, and finally secretary to General Acquaviva, who detailed him to write the Jesuit Order's history. That work covers only Saint Ignatius's generalate.

Edited by Sacchini, it appeared as Historiae Societatis Jesu prima pars at Rome in 1614, 1615 and 1621, Antwerp in 1620, and Cologne in 1620. Written as annals, it rests chiefly on a life by the saint's secretary de Polanco. Ranke praised Orlandini as exceedingly careful, accurate and wary in style and business. Sacchini, Possinus, Jouvancy and Cordara continued the history, its sixth and last part, reaching 1633, appearing at Rome in 1758. His Life of Peter Faber was translated into French and Italian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-just:
Nicholas Justiniani, birth date unknown, became a monk in Venice's Benedictine monastery of San Niccolo del Lido in 1153. When a 1172 Venetian military expedition wiped out all other Justiniani in the Aegean near Chios, the Republic mourned the noble family's disaster as a public calamity. Lest the family die out entirely, Venice sent Baron Morosin and Toma Falier to Alexander III, seeking dispensation from Nicholas's monastic vows.

With the dispensation granted, Nicholas married Anna, daughter of Doge Michieli, and fathered five new branches of the family through her. Shortly after 1179 he returned to San Niccolo del Lido, having first founded a women's convent on Aniano island, where his wife took the veil. Both died with a reputation for holiness and were honoured by the people, though the Church never formally beatified either.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-papi:
Nicholas Papini, historian, was born at San Giovanni Valdarno, between Florence and Arezzo, about 1751 and died at Terni, Umbria, on 16 December 1834. Entering the Conventual Order, he taught Italian literature at Modena. He served as secretary of Tuscany's Provincial, custos of Assisi's Sacred Convent from about 1800 to 1803, and briefly guardian of Rome's Dodici Apostoli. He was finally Minister General of the Conventuals from 1803 to 1809.

Later he lived at Assisi and Terni, where he lies buried. His printed works include L'Etruria Francescana, a collection of history notes on Tuscany's Conventual Franciscans, published at Siena in 1797. Notizie sicure, on Saint Francis's death, burial, canonisation and body's discovery, reached a second edition at Foligno in 1824. Storia del Perdono d'Assisi, with papers, appeared at Florence in 1824. La Storia di San Francesco d'Assisi, a critical work in two volumes, appeared at Foligno in 1827.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicola-avanci:
Nicola Avancini, a Jesuit writer born in the Tyrol in 1612, spent his life teaching and governing colleges across central Europe. He held chairs in rhetoric, philosophy, and theology at Graz and Vienna, led colleges at Passau, Vienna, and Graz, and served as provincial of Austria.

Among many books on philosophy, theology, and sacred letters, only his meditations on the life and teaching of Jesus stayed widely read. Translated into the main European languages, they went through many editions and guided daily prayer for generations. His sermons, orations, and many college dramas fill out a list the entry points readers to in Sommervogel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolo-albert:
Dominican statesman Nicolo Albertini, born at Prato, rose from a Florence convent to the highest ranks of the medieval church. Joining the Dominicans at sixteen in 1266 and studying at Paris, he preached widely, governed houses of his order, and became its procurator-general.

Boniface VIII made him bishop of Spoleto in 1299 and sent him to reconcile Philip IV of France with Edward I of England, a mission he carried through. Benedict XI then raised him to dean of the Sacred College and cardinal-bishop of Ostia, posts he held until his death at Avignon in 1321.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nocera-dei-pa:
Nocera dei Pagani, a diocese below Mount Albino on the Sarno in southern Italy, bears a name from a ninth-century Saracen colony. Ancient Nuceria Alfaterna, taken by Fabius Maximus in 307 BC and sacked by Hannibal, later saw King Roger nearly raze it and Charles of Durazzo besiege Urban VI within its walls.

The town birthed Hugh of Payns, a founder of the Templars, and the painter Francesco Solimena, and Alphonsus Liguori founded his order there. Its sanctuary of Mater Domini holds the tomb of Charles I of Anjou, and bishops from Saint Priscus onward fill its list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ordines-roman:
Ordines Romani, or Roman ordines, are medieval ritual books that direct liturgical action without printing the prayers themselves. Sacramentary, antiphonary, and psalter held the texts, while the ordo gave ceremonial alone, sometimes for one rite like baptism or church consecration, sometimes for many rites together.

Amalarius in the ninth century already cites writings containing the Roman order in separate booklets, and manuscripts from the eighth to twelfth centuries preserve many ordines. After the twelfth century the name yielded to ceremonial and ordinary, except for the daily directory of office and Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orsini:
The Orsini were one of Rome's oldest and most powerful noble houses, and their story runs through much of medieval Italian history. From a Roman main line that split into many branches, the family held wide lands, walled towns, and strongholds across Italy. As papal champions heading the Guelph party, they stood through generations against their rivals, the Colonna, who backed the emperor.

Three popes came from the house, Celestine III, Nicholas III, and Benedict XIII, along with many cardinals, bishops, and prelates. Other Orsini won fame as soldiers, statesmen, artists, and scholars. The entry follows the family line by line, naming its cardinals and princes in turn, and shows how its feuds and alliances helped shape Rome and the Papal States over centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palatini:
Palatini, from the Latin palatium for palace, first meant high officials of the papal court. In the Middle Ages the judices palatini served as the top officers of the papal household, and they grew weighty as the popes' temporal power grew. Two superintendents of papal notaries headed the list, running official papers, judicial inquiries, and the Lateran archives.

Other palatini included the nomenculator, who handled petitions to the pope. The arcarius and saccellarius served as chief treasurers of the Lateran Palace. The primicerius and secundicerius of the defensores aided widows, orphans, captives, and other needy folk. The entry traces how these offices grew from late Roman court posts, changed across the ninth century, and faded as the papal household took modern shape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paolo-agostin:
Paolo Agostini was an Italian composer born at Vallerano in 1593 and dead in 1629, pupil and son-in-law of the famed Nanini. Taking Venetian and Roman masters as models, he studied above all the art of writing for many choirs at once, and won the highest esteem of his age. After hearing a Mass of his for forty-eight voices, Pope Urban VIII voiced his highest admiration.

Manuscript copies of his works lie in the Vatican Archives and the Corsini Library. Only a few reached print: two volumes of Psalms in 1619, two of Magnificats in 1620, and five volumes of Masses for four to twelve voices from 1624 to 1628. He succeeded Ugolini as master of the Vatican Chapel in 1627. Elegant and ingenious throughout, his work could rise to lofty genius, as in an Agnus Dei reprinted by Martini.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paolo-ruffini:
Paolo Ruffini was a physician and mathematician born at Valentano on 3 September 1765 and dead at Modena on 10 May 1822. He first meant to take holy orders and even received the tonsure, but turned to mathematics and medicine at Modena University, where he took his doctorate. At twenty-three he became professor of analysis, after a year deputising for his teacher Cassiani, and in 1791 took the chair of elementary mathematics.

During the French invasion of 1796 he sat in the legislative body at Milan, then struggled home to his Modena lectures. He lost his public chair for refusing the republican oath without a conscience clause, and regained it with the Austrians in 1799. He declined Pavia's higher chair to keep his Modena medical practice, and in 1806 took applied mathematics at the new military school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paolo-vergani:
Paolo Vergani was an Italian political economist born in Piedmont in 1753 and dead at Paris about 1820. As a student he bent to church and civil law and history, won distinction in theology, took orders, and went to Rome to study further, soon becoming canon of Saint John Lateran. There he wrote on the death penalty, criminal justice, and duelling, winning a high place among eighteenth-century jurists.

Those writings likely won him posts as assessor general of finance and commerce and inspector of agriculture and the arts. His 1791 work on the Papal States' finances under Pius VI backs import duties to shield home industry, denying that farming alone can source a state's wealth. He appeals to religion and Christian charity, urging protection for home trades that employ many, while manufactures and imports employ few.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parabolani:
The Parabolani were a brotherhood who in the early Church freely took on care of the sick and burial of the dead. Their name comes from risking their lives, paraballesthai ten zoen, by facing contagious disease. Some claim the brotherhood formed in Alexandria's great plague under Dionysius the Great, though proof is thin. Besides works of mercy they served as the bishop's bodyguard.

Their numbers stayed small. The Theodosian Code of 416 capped Alexandria's roll at 500, a law two years later raised it to 600, and Justinian's Code cut Constantinople's from 1,100 to 950. They vanish after Justinian. Chosen by the bishop and under his control, they also answered to the prefect Augustalis. They held no orders or vows, yet counted among clergy with clerical privileges. Law barred them from public gatherings and theatres.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-maroni:
Paul Maroni was a Jesuit missionary born on 1 November 1695. He joined the Austrian Jesuit province on 27 October 1712, and in 1723, like many German and Austrian missionaries of the day, sailed for the Upper Maranon mission of the Quito province. After years teaching theology at Quito, he worked with great success among Indians on the Napo and Aguarico rivers, converting tribes and founding new reductions, or settlements of converted Indians.

At the same time he carefully explored those regions, work French geographer La Condamine duly praised in 1750. Maroni left valuable writings, only lately printed. One is his 1737 diary of an entry by the Pastaza River, printed at Quito in 1895. Another is his Authentic News of the Famous Maranon River and Quito's apostolic mission, printed at Madrid in 1889 with maps of his own drawing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-berret:
Pietro Berrettini, called Pietro da Cortona, was an Italian painter, architect, and writer of the Baroque age. He was born at Cortona in 1596 and trained under his uncle and at Florence. He reached Rome at fifteen and studied Raphael, Michelangelo, and the reliefs of Trajan's Column.

His triumph was the great ceiling of the Barberini Palace, an allegory of that family's history. Work at Saint Peter's followed, then frescoes for the Pitti Palace in Florence, where jealous rivals drove him away before the series was done. Knighted by Alexander VII and buried in San Martino, a church he designed, he left pupils who carried his grand manner across Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poggio-bracci:
Poggio Bracciolini was an Italian humanist whose searches through monastery libraries recovered lost treasures of Latin literature. He was born at Terranuova near Arezzo in 1380 and studied at Florence. He went to Rome about 1402 and served as apostolic secretary under a succession of popes.

Leisure during the Council of Constance let him hunt manuscripts in Germany and France. At Cluny in 1415 he found speeches of Cicero, and at Saint Gall the first complete Quintilian. Later journeys yielded Lucretius, Ammianus Marcellinus, Vitruvius, and more. Most survive only in copies, but his finds reshaped Renaissance knowledge of Rome's writers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prospero-alpi:
Prospero Alpini, physician and plant scholar, was born at Marostica on 23 November 1553. He died at Padua on 6 February 1617. He studied medicine at Padua from 1574 to 1578. Then he spent two years at Campo San Pietro. In 1580 he sailed to Egypt as doctor to the Venetian consul. Egypt gave him the chance he wanted: to study plants in a warmer climate than Italy offered.

Back in Venice in 1586, he served Andrea Doria, Prince of Melfi. In Genoa he won a name as the leading physician of his day. Returning to Padua in 1593, he held the botany chair for many years. His Latin books on Egyptian plants and Egyptian medicine made his fame. The medicine volume of 1591 is said to hold the first mention of the coffee plant by a European writer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prospero-fagn:
Prospero Fagnani, Italian canon lawyer, died in 1678. His birth year is disputed, with writers giving 1598, 1587 or 1588. He studied at Perugia. He became a doctor of civil and canon law at twenty. At twenty-two he took up the secretaryship of the Congregation of the Council. He held that post for fifteen years. He later served other Roman congregations in the same role.

Blind from the age of forty-four, Fagnani kept working. He produced a commentary on the Decretals of Gregory the Ninth. It earned him the nickname of the blind yet keen-sighted doctor. The commentary untangles some of the hardest texts in that collection. In one famous passage he attacked probabilism, the view that a doubtful opinion may be followed. Saint Alphonsus later called him the great prince of the rigorists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raneiro-sacch:
Raneiro Sacchoni was a learned Dominican, born at Piacenza about the start of the thirteenth century and dead about 1263. This encyclopedia entry corrects the common dates of 1258 or 1259 for his death. A Brief of Urban the Fourth, calling him to Rome on 21 July 1262, proves he lived past those years. By his own avowal, he was perverted by the Cathari at an early age, became one of their bishops, and stayed among them seventeen years.

Preaching by Saint Peter Martyr most likely led him back to the faith. He joined the Order of Preachers, then newly founded, and laboured zealously among the heretics of Upper Italy. After Peter's martyrdom he became inquisitor for Lombardy and the Marches of Ancona. His Summa against the Waldenses counted as an authority through the Middle Ages, though the Gretser edition of 1738 is interpolated. Echard, Hunter and Touron supply the entry's sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-marti:
Raymond Martini, Dominican theologian and Orientalist, was born at Subirats in Catalonia about 1220 and died after July 1284. This encyclopedia entry tells that in 1250 his superiors chose him to study Oriental languages. In 1264 he joined the commission Jaime the First of Aragon named to censure the writings held by Jews, and afterwards preached to the Moors in Spain and Tunis. Returning to Barcelona in 1269, he taught Oriental languages with success and wrote against Jews and Moors.

His chief work, Pugio Fidei Christianae, finished after 1278 and printed at Paris in 1651 and Leipzig in 1687, is in Latin and Hebrew. It argues from Hebrew scripture and old rabbinical writings that Christianity is true against the Jews. The work shows Martini extremely well read in Hebrew literature, and scholars prize it for its citations from the Talmud and other sources. The Jewish Encyclopedia and the Journal of Philology appear among the entry's references.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rimini:
Rimini is a diocese on Italy's Adriatic coast, suffragan to Ravenna, set between the Marecchia and Ausa rivers. Fishing and coastal trade were its chief industries. Its thirteenth-century cathedral, San Francesco, was reshaped by Sigismondo Malatesta in 1446-55 to designs by Leone Battista Alberti and never finished, lacking cupola and upper facade. Inside lie the tombs of Sigismondo and his wife Isotta, with decorations by Agostino di Duccio and a fresco by Piero della Francesca.

History runs deep here. Built by the Umbri and taken by Gauls, Rimini became a Latin colony in 263 BC and a loyal Roman ally. Augustus adorned it with an arch and a five-arched bridge. Goths, Byzantines, and Lombards fought over it in turn, Pepin gave it to the Holy See, and in the thirteenth century the Malatesta rose to power. The entry also notes its town hall gallery and Gambalunga Library of 1677.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-segni:
Segni, a hill town in the Lepini mountains above the Sacco valley, keeps traces of a very old past. A double ring of massive stone wall still stands there. One gate has a lintel made from a single great block. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows the town from its days as a colony under Tarquin the Proud, through repeated revolts against Rome, to its later role as a refuge for popes. Eugenius III built a palace there.

Bishops anchor the second half, from Sanctulus around 494 through Saint Bruno the scriptural commentator. One bishop was deposed for backing an antipope and later restored. Thomas Becket was canonized in the cathedral in 1173. The entry closes by noting Segni as the birthplace of Pope Saint Vitalian and a noted physician, and by giving the diocese's parishes and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simone-martin:
Simone Martini, also called Simone di Martino and Simone Memmi, was a Sienese painter born at Siena in 1283, dead either there or at Avignon in 1344 or 1349. He is now judged a direct pupil of Duccio, whom he surpassed in decorative quality. His earliest authentic work is the great fresco of the enthroned Virgin and Child at Siena, painted in 1315 and restored by himself in 1321 after damp damage.

In 1320 he painted an altarpiece for Saint Catherine's at Pisa, now broken up. The next year he worked at Orvieto for Saint Dominic's, then returned to Siena for his splendid 1328 portrait of Fogliano, honoring the capture of Montemassi. Later he painted at Assisi a series on Saint Martin's life, and spent his last years at Avignon in papal service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-andrew-cor:
St. Andrew Corsini, of the illustrious Florentine family, was born in 1302 and died in 1373, a wild youth turned Carmelite bishop and peacemaker. This entry tells how his mother's words about events before his birth startled him out of dissipation into the Carmelite order in his native city. Where he began a life of great mortification, studied at Paris and Avignon. And on returning became the apostle of Florence, regarded as prophet and wonder-worker.

Called to the see of Fiesole, he fled, was found by a child. And compelled to accept, redoubling his austerities as bishop, lavishing care on the poor. And serving everywhere as peacemaker, notably at Bologna as papal legate between nobility and people. After twelve years as bishop he died at seventy-one, with miracles multiplying at his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-jerome-emi:
Jerome Emiliani, founder of the Somaschans, turned soldier and prisoner into father of plague orphans. Born at Venice in 1481 to Angelo Emiliani, called Miani, and Eleonore Mauroceni, he joined the army and defended Castelnuovo against Cambrai's League in 1508. Taken prisoner and miraculously freed, he walked to Treviso's shrine of Our Lady in fulfilment of a vow. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Somascha to 8 February 1537.

Podestà of Castelnuovo briefly, he returned to Venice to oversee his nephews' education, giving spare time to theology and charity. Ordained in 1518, hospitals and hovels became his haunts. In plague and famine year 1528 he seemed everywhere, above all for orphans, whose numbers had swelled. He rented a house for them near St. Rose's church, aided by pious laymen, and took charge of Cajetan's hospital for incurables. From that work grew his order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-sylvester-:
Sylvester Gozzolini, founder of the Sylvestrines, left law and a canonry for a hermit's poverty in the Marche. Born at Osimo in 1177 to the noble Gozzolini, he studied jurisprudence at Bologna and Padua, then abandoned law for theology, Scripture, and long daily prayer. His father, angered at the change, refused to speak to him for ten years.

A canon at Osimo, he rebuked his bishop's scandalous life and faced loss of his canonry. Seeing the decaying corpse of a once beautiful person, he left the world. In 1227 he retired to a desert place thirty miles from Osimo, moved to Grotta Fucile, and built a monastery there. His order of Benedictine hermits spread through Italy. He died on 26 November 1267.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-veronica-g:
Veronica Giuliani, a Capuchin mystic of Città di Castello, bore the stigmata and wrote a vast diary of her spiritual life. Born Ursula Giuliani at Mercatello in Urbino in 1660 to Francesco Giuliana and Benedetta Mancini, she showed marvels of sanctity from infancy. At eighteen months she reportedly rebuked a shopman serving false measure of oil: Do justice, God sees you.

At three she received divine communications and gave food and clothes to poor children. A vision of her heart as steel cured a dictatorial streak at sixteen. Entering the Capuchins, she lived in austerity, received the wounds of Christ, and served as abbess for eleven years. Her diary runs to thousands of pages. She died at Città di Castello on 9 July 1727 and was canonised in 1839.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sylvester-maz:
Sylvester Mazzolini, born at Priero in Piedmont in 1460, was a Dominican theologian and the first writer to attack Luther in print. He joined the Dominicans at fifteen and taught theology at Bologna, Pavia, and Rome. Julius II called him to Rome in 1511. He served as Master of the Sacred Palace from 1515 until his death in 1523.

His writings ranged over planets, demons, history, homiletics, Aquinas, and papal primacy. Luther answered his arguments, and a regular controversy followed, whose haste explains some roughness of style. Chief works include his 1520 defence of Rome's authority and his replies to Luther of 1519 and 1520. The Summa Summarum of 1516 was reprinted forty times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodosius-fl:
Swiss Capuchin Theodosius Florentini stood up for Catholics when Radical rule pressed them hard. Born at Münster in the Grisons on 23 May 1808, he died at Heiden in Appenzell on 15 February 1865. He joined the Capuchin Franciscans on 22 October 1825, was made priest in 1830, and taught novices, philosophy, and theology.

Baden made him guardian in 1838, Chur made him superior and parish priest in 1845, definitor in 1857, and vicar-general of Chur in 1860. Swiss Catholics faced Protestant rule, unbelief, false mysticism, and even Catholic cantons harrying convents. The Sonderbund war broke Catholic strength, Radicals set up a league sworn to crush Catholic interests, and his bold defence drove Theodosius to flee to Alsace in 1841.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-tambur:
Thomas Tamburini, a moral theologian born at Caltanisetta, Sicily, in 1591, taught and ruled Jesuit colleges across a long career, dying at Palermo in 1675. He entered the Society of Jesus at fifteen and proved a gifted teacher. He held chairs in philosophy for four years, dogmatic theology for seven, and moral theology for seventeen, besides thirteen years as rector of various colleges.

His books went through several editions. They include a five-volume Method of Ready Confession in 1647, works on Communion, the Decalogue and the Mass, and a three-volume exposition of divine, natural and church law. Severe with himself, he took the milder view for others when reputable authors allowed it, a stance that drew charges of laxity and a sharp exchange with Vincent Baron. Alphonsus Liguori later urged readers not to underrate him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tommasso-gior:
Tommaso Giordani, a composer born at Naples in 1738, spent most of his life in Dublin, where he died in February 1806. His family reached London in 1752 and settled in Dublin in 1764. Giordani led the musical life of the Irish capital from 1764 to 1781, returned to London for two years, then came back to Dublin for good.

He ran an opera house and a music shop, neither of which paid well. His works include many operas, the oratorio Isaac of 1767, and a mass of overtures, sonatas, concertos, quartets and songs. He served as organist of the pro-cathedral from 1784 to 1798, conducted his own Te Deum for George III's recovery in April 1789, and taught Lady Morgan and Tom Cooke. John Field, inventor of the nocturne, made his debut at one of Giordani's Rotunda concerts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trapani:
A diocese in Sicily, suffragan of Palermo, set on a hook-shaped tongue of land at the island's western tip. The shape gave the ancient town its name, Drepanon, meaning reaping-hook. The city keeps a good harbour trading wine, tunny-fish, salt and worked coral, alabaster and mother-of-pearl.

Its fortress-like cathedral holds paintings by Careca and Van Dyck, including a Crucifixion, and an alabaster Dead Christ by Tartaglia. The entry also names the Annunziata sanctuary's great Madonna, attributed to Nicolò Pisano. Native sons include the painters Carrera and Errante, the mathematician Ximenes and the musician Scarlatti.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-victimae-pasc:
Victimae Paschali Laudes is the Easter sequence, the chant that follows the Epistle at Easter Mass, assigned by the Roman Missal daily from Easter through the following Saturday. Medieval missals placed it on various days of the octave, but Rome fixed its week-long use.

Authorship is ascribed, on an eleventh-century Einsiedeln manuscript, to Wipo, with weaker claims for Notker Balbulus, King Robert II of France. Adam of St Victor, the last impossible since manuscripts predate his birth. Hymnologically it matters as a bridge: sharing Notker's varying stanza forms and casual assonance, it advances toward regular rhyme and stanza, and remains the only quasi-Notkerian sequence kept in the Missal. The entry also notes a 1908 textual restoration, suos for vos, in its Galilee line.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vineam-domini:
Vineam Domini, the Lord's Vineyard, is an apostolic constitution issued by Clement XI against the Jansenists on 16 July 1705. It arose from a case of conscience put by a Jansenist priest, ostensibly confessor to a dying cleric, to doctors of the Sorbonne: could absolution be given to a priest who rejected? In the Church's sense, the five propositions condemned as Jansenist, yet, unsure they truly appeared in Jansenius's Augustinus, thought respectful silence enough while signing Alexander VII's formula?

Forty Sorbonne doctors, including Ellies Du Pin and Natalis Alexander, secretly decided in July 1701 that absolution could not be withheld. Since the case was neither new nor extraordinary and the penitent's opinion was not condemned. The Jansenists published the case with the doctors' signatures in July 1702. Clement's constitution answered by rejecting respectful silence as a sufficient submission to the Church's judgment on fact as well as doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilhelm-lamor:
Wilhelm Lamormaini was a Jesuit priest who served as spiritual adviser to Emperor Ferdinand II during the Thirty Years War era. Born at Dochamps in Luxemburg in 1570, he died at Vienna in 1648. He studied at Trier and Prague, joined the Jesuits in 1590, and taught at Graz before leading Jesuit colleges at Graz and Vienna. From 1643 to 1645 he headed the Austrian branch of his order, stepping down when gout made travel too hard.

Court life gave him wide sway over imperial policy, and critics joked that Jesuits rather than the emperor ruled. He pushed recovered church lands toward Catholic missions after the 1629 Edict of Restitution, took part in moves against Wallenstein, and backed the Counter-Reformation across Austria, Styria, Bohemia, and Moravia. Late in life he founded a Vienna fund for poor students. Part of his life of Ferdinand II reached print in 1638.

dyke-darrel-the-railroad-detective-or-th:
Dyke Darrel the Railroad Detective, or the Crime of the Midnight Express, by Frank Pinkerton and dated 1886, is a dime novel of train crime. Pinkerton's contents open with a startling crime and the detective's first trick, then introduce Professor Darlington Ruggles. A scalping, a rebuff, and the detective in danger follow at chapter speed, with a handkerchief supplying the clue that turns the case.

Later headings promise a plunge to death, Black Hollow, a burning trap, and Nell missing and in the toils. A baffled villain, a sad fate, and a girl who outmatches the detective himself round out the bill. Railroad detectives were real officers of the new rail corporations, guarding expresses and payrolls, and Pinkerton's hero does that work at melodrama pitch, one chapter ending per cliff edge.
eugenics-and-other-evils-an-argument-aga: Eugenics and Other Evils, G. K. Chesterton's argument against the scientifically organized state. The anti-eugenic polemic. This book preserves that essay. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
forty-centuries-of-ink-or-a-chronologica:
David N. Carvalho spent forty centuries in one book, tracing ink from ancient Egypt to the chemical laboratory. Carvalho marches through classical, medieval, and Renaissance inks, then studies recipes, classifications, and the utensils of writing, from reed pens and quills to steel nibs and pencils. Papyrus, parchment, vellum, and true paper get chapters as ink's backgrounds, the surfaces it sits on.

The last part turns legal: official ink, enduring ink, fraudulent ink, and chemico-legal ink, meaning ink tested as courtroom evidence. Carvalho warns that most modern inks fade fast, a danger to records. History, chemistry, anecdotes, and poetry crowd together in an enthusiast's survey of a humble substance.
govdocs-archive_org-nihilism-franco-volp:
Franco Volpi, an Italian philosopher, wrote Nihilism as a history of one of philosophy's darkest concepts. He develops an earlier synopsis of the problem into a full account, following nihilism from its roots in German idealism onward.

The story runs through Nietzsche, who named nihilism as Europe's coming crisis, and into the twentieth century, where the collapse of old values became a central theme of thought. Volpi writes as a historian of ideas, tracing who used the word and what each meant by it. The book suits readers of continental philosophy who want the concept's whole career.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CommunistInvolv:
On June 9, 1964, the FBI's San Francisco office sent this confidential memorandum concerning Lee Harvey Oswald. It belongs to the Bureau's Oswald file at the height of the Warren Commission's work, when every office's holdings on the accused assassin were being gathered and summarized.

The archive's filing label ties the memo to the question of alleged Communist involvement. That was the charge the Bureau had tracked since Oswald's defection to the Soviet Union in 1959 and his return with a Russian wife. Memos of this kind weighed his Marxism, his contacts, and his committees. The single memo is preserved as a page of the Bureau's political file on Oswald.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GeorgetownUnive:
Tabitha Petran wrote an article charging Georgetown University with a part in government sponsored fascism. Her subject is the university's role in training occupational police and administrators. In her account, an American campus helped prepare the men who would run occupied or allied territory for Washington.

The charge ties a respected university to the machinery of empire. Training programs look neutral on a catalog page, and Petran asks readers to see the politics inside them. Her article preserves a sharp left critique of how American power staffed itself after the war.
govdocs-archive_org-the-mystery-of-the-h: Luis Felipe Moyano Cires, writing as Nimrod de Rosario, cast his teaching as a magical novel, The Mystery of Belicena Villca. It is also titled The Mystery of the Hyperborean Wisdom. Hyperborea, a perfect land beyond the north wind, anchors his esoteric system. The library holds the volume as an archive item, without backing. It serves the study of modern esoteric movements and their use of fiction as scripture.
madame-firmiani:
Madame Firmiani is a short tale by Honoré de Balzac, in Katharine Wormeley's translation. Balzac dedicated it to his old friend Alexandre de Berny. His opening pages muse on stories that only the heart can tell. Some portraits, he says, need an infusion of soul to live.

Madame Firmiani is a beautiful widow at the center of Paris gossip. A young man loves her, while rumors say her fortune is ruined. Balzac peels away the world's false account of her. Her true story proves nobler and sadder than the talk. The tale belongs to his great Human Comedy. It glitters with Parisian air and quiet moral force.
massimilla-doni:
Honore de Balzac wrote Massimilla Doni, here in English by Clara Bell and James Waring. A note to Jacques Strunz opens the book. Balzac thanks Strunz for teaching him the craft behind fine music.

Venice fills the first pages, with its old and proud noble houses. Balzac says that glory has sunk into ruin and want. Gondoliers now serve the English, though some bear names older than kings. Love and opera grow from that rich, faded ground. Balzac's note admits his guide knew far more of music than he did. That debt shapes the tale's deep care for song and stage.
nasa-tm-19660021864-asee-university-of-m:
A final report dated January 1966 closes a summer fellowship program that joined the American Society for Engineering Education with two universities and NASA. Faculty fellows from the University of Maryland and Catholic University spent a summer working on NASA research. The report is filed from Goddard under number X-520-66-3. Its catalog note lists the fellows' project areas one by one.

Holography, an infrared laser, and a digital filter appear among the projects. Antenna tracking accuracy, PCM telemetry, and an optical tracking control system are also named. Summer programs of this kind moved ideas between campuses and the space agency. The final report preserves what one summer's fellows attempted, as a record for both sides.
pausanias-the-spartan-the-haunted-and-th:
Pausanias, the Spartan is an unfinished historical romance by Edward Bulwer-Lytton, edited after his death by his son. The son's dedication letter explains that Lytton began the work fifteen or twenty years earlier and kept returning to it. The subject haunted his imagination and was never abandoned.

Pausanias, regent of Sparta, built a vast conspiracy known only in brief from Thucydides and Plutarch. Had it succeeded, his son notes, it would have changed history. The volume pairs the fragment with Lytton's ghost story "The Haunted and the Haunters," two works from opposite ends of his art.

schiller-wallenstein-coleridge-1800-picc:
S T Coleridge's translation of Schiller's Wallenstein, Part 1: The Piccolomini, appeared in 1800. Friedrich Schiller's Wallenstein trilogy was the great German historical drama of its age. Coleridge, the English poet, translated two parts during his stay in Germany and made them his own in English verse.

The Piccolomini sets the stage in the Thirty Years' War, where General Wallenstein's army waits and wonders at his plans. Young Max Piccolomini loves Wallenstein's daughter while his father plots against the general. Loyalty, ambition, and star lore hang over the camp scenes. Coleridge's version was a turning point for English Romantic drama, proof that German theater could live in English.
the-concept-of-nature-the-tarner-lecture:
Alfred North Whitehead delivered these lectures at Trinity College in November 1919, as the first course of Tarner lectures. A transcriber's note explains the handling of mathematical notation, with carets for superscripts, underscores for subscripts, and Greek letters written out. Two printer's errors, the note adds, have been corrected by sense.

Whitehead's preface explains the lectureship itself. It is an occasional office founded by the generosity of Mr. Edward Tarner. Each holder's duty is to deliver a course on the philosophy of the sciences and the relations between them, as the preface begins to state. Whitehead's course takes the concept of nature as its theme. That means asking what nature is as an object of thought, apart from the mind that thinks it. The lectures became a landmark in his philosophy, and the plain preface, with its thanks to the founder, sets the formal frame for a demanding argument.

un-un-res-report-of-the-secretary-genera:
Ground rules for the United Nations Emergency Force in Egypt are laid down in this 1956 report of the Secretary-General, document A/3375. The force was the first of its kind, sent during the Suez Crisis to stand between armies. Egypt's consent, and clear limits on the force, were the price of its welcome.

The report states that the force would enter only with Egypt's agreement and would not fight except in self-defense. It covers freedom of movement, ties to local authorities, and the force's neutral role. These basic points became core doctrine for peacekeeping around the world.
zanoni:
Edward Bulwer Lytton wrote this occult novel, framed here by his 1845 dedicatory letter to sculptor John Gibson. Lytton praises Gibson for living apart from rivalry and greed. Gibson works in Rome among the loveliest remains of the past, he writes. Fame without a desire for gold marks the true artist. That ideal, Lytton says, matches the principle the novel seeks to convey.

The letter sets a high, serious tone before the tale begins. Hidden wisdom and spiritual aspiration drive Zanoni's story of an immortal adept. Readers get Rosicrucian mystery mixed with love and sacrifice. Lytton's praise of Canova's pupil also preserves a glimpse of Rome's art world.
